title: Write-Back Pattern
description: Explore write-back (write-behind) caching, where writes are committed to Redis first and flushed to the database asynchronously.

data.text: Write-back caching, also called write-behind, reverses the normal write priority. Instead of updating the database first, the application writes to Redis and returns immediately. A background process later flushes accumulated writes to the database. This decouples the user-facing write latency from the database write latency.

When a write request arrives, the application stores the new value in Redis with a special marker or in a dedicated write queue. The HTTP response is sent immediately. A separate background worker, running on a timer or triggered by queue length, reads pending writes and applies them to the database in batches.

data.title: Write flow:
items: Application writes the new value to Redis and marks it as dirty.
Redis acknowledges the write and the application returns success.
A background worker polls Redis for dirty keys or reads from a write queue.
The worker applies the pending writes to the database.
After a successful database write, the dirty marker is removed.

data.text: Reads always query Redis because it holds the latest written data. The database is treated as a durable archive rather than the live source of truth. If the background worker fails, dirty data remains in Redis and can be retried later without data loss.

data.caption: Write-back background flush flow
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Redis
    participant Worker
    participant DB
    App->>Redis: SET product:10 <new-data>
    Redis-->>App: OK
    Note over App: Response returned immediately
    loop Every 2 seconds
        Worker->>Redis: Get dirty keys
        Redis-->>Worker: [product:10]
        Worker->>DB: UPDATE Products SET ... WHERE Id = 10
        DB-->>Worker: OK
        Worker->>Redis: REM dirty:product:10

Data Loss Risk
data.text: If Redis crashes before the background worker flushes dirty writes, those writes are lost because they never reached the database. Write-back is not suitable for data that cannot be recreated.

terms.definition: A Redis key whose value has changed but has not yet been persisted to the database.
A Redis set or list used to track keys that need to be flushed to the database by the background worker.
A consistency model where the database eventually catches up with the cache, but readers may see stale data during the flush window.

items.question: What is the biggest downside of write-back?
items.answer: The risk of data loss if Redis fails before dirty writes are flushed. It is only appropriate for data that can be recreated or rebuilt.

items.question: How large should the flush interval be?
items.answer: It depends on your durability requirements. A shorter interval reduces data-loss exposure but increases database load. Typical values range from 1 to 30 seconds.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Write-back decouples write latency from the database.
Redis is the live source of truth; the database lags behind.
A background worker batches and flushes dirty writes.
Data loss is possible if Redis fails before flushing.
data.takeaway: Write-back maximizes write throughput and is ideal for write-intensive, non-critical workloads.

data.title: Build a Write-Back Logger
data.description: Application logs are written at high volume. Durability is less important than throughput.
steps: Create a Redis write queue for log entries.
Write incoming log entries to Redis and add their keys to a dirty set.
Run a background flush every 3 seconds that bulk-inserts into the database.
Simulate a Redis restart and measure how many entries are lost.
Add a cap on the dirty set size to bound memory usage.
data.expectedOutcome: Log writes return immediately, and the database receives batched inserts on the flush schedule.
